title: Diversity Over Frequency: Rethinking Tool Use in Visual Chain-of-Thought Agents
claim: Standard and tool-encouraged training under-explore and collapse to wrong answers, while diversity-encouraged training explores broadly and succeeds even when tools are dropped.
layout: 3 columns by 2 rows, early over late phase, red ✗ versus green ✓
description: A question banner sits at the top: which object the man is facing, the dressing room or the baby. Below it are three columns: Vanilla RFT, Tool-Encouraged RFT and Diversity-Encouraged RFT. The top row, shaded blue, is the early training phase. Each column shows the same photo of a man beside a red stroller, with arrows fanning out to N zoom or crop rollouts. Each rollout has a text snippet and a cropped image. In the first two columns the red boxes overlap on the face, and the caption reads Limited Exploration. In the third column, green boxes cover the face, the stroller and the doors, and the caption reads Sufficient Exploration. The bottom row, shaded green, is the late training phase. It shows reasoning traces: red text and an ✗ for the first two columns, green text and a ✓ for the third. The labels are Tool-Use Collapse, Always Tool-Use and Tool as Scaffolding. The eye goes first to the red-versus-green contrast.
caption: Effect of Early Exploration on the Late Training Phase. This figure compares agent behaviors in the early training (top) and late training (bottom) phases. Both vanilla (Left) and tool-encouraged RFT (Middle) suffer from limited early exploration in both text and visual modalities. This lack of rollout diversity restricts models to local optima with marginal gains regardless of tool usage frequency. In contrast, encouraging exploration (Right) leads to better performance even when the agent rarely uses tools. We call this the scaffolding effect where early tool use acts like temporary supports to build reasoning capabilities that remain effective even after tool use is discarded.
abstract: Visual agents employ external visual tools within visual chains of thought to incorporate fine-grained evidence. While prior work has mainly studied these tools in visual search tasks, their role in more complex visual reasoning remains underexplored. In this paper, we move beyond simple visual search tasks to investigate more challenging tasks, including 3D spatial reasoning and medical visual question answering, where agents must integrate tool-acquired local evidence with the global context. We identify a {tool-use collapse phenomenon: models progressively stop using tools while still achieving higher task accuracy. Moreover, we observe a clear asymmetry: (i) completely eliminating tool use degrades performance, whereas (ii) incentivizing tool use yields only marginal gains despite substantially increasing usage. We find that vanilla training and tool-use encouragement both reduce rollout diversity, explaining why higher tool use does not yield stronger reasoning performance. Motivated by these findings, we add an entropy regularization term to encourage diverse rollout exploration, achieving the best performance despite gradually declining tool usage. Overall, our findings suggest a training-time view of tools as scaffolding, where broader exploration over language generation and visual tool invocation improves reasoning despite tool-use collapse. Project page: https://scaffolded-exploration.github.io
